candidate.stem: A hospital deploys the identical diagnostic AI system in two settings. In the first, it only flags anomalies for a radiologist who makes every final call. In the second, it independently orders follow-up tests and finalizes reports, with a human reviewing only a periodic sample. The system's underlying capability score is unchanged between the two settings. What follows about the risk of each deployment?

options.text: The two deployments carry different risk exposure even though the system's capability is identical, because how much of the task the AI is allowed to do on its own is a separate, deployment-time choice, not a property of the system's capability.
The second deployment is inherently more dangerous than the first, because letting an AI act with less human oversight is inherently more dangerous regardless of what changes in practice.
options.provenance: conflates autonomy level with inherent danger directly, missing that autonomy level affects risk exposure rather than being dangerous in itself

options.text: Since the system is clearly capable enough to work with minimal oversight, using it under close supervision in the first setting wastes its capability and is itself the unsafe choice.
options.provenance: misreads 'higher capability levels unlock higher autonomy' as capability requiring or mandating high autonomy, rather than merely making it possible while lower autonomy remains available

options.text: The system's underlying capability must actually be higher in the second setting, since operating with only periodic human review requires more capability than operating under full human control.
options.provenance: misreads a change in deployment autonomy as necessarily reflecting a change in capability, when the stem stipulates capability is held constant and autonomy is set independently by the deployer

candidate.explanation: Autonomy describes how a task is divided between human and AI at deployment time; capability describes what the system can do. Holding capability fixed while varying autonomy is exactly this case: a capable system deployed as a tool can be safer than the same system deployed as an agent, even though the underlying capability is identical. Distractor 1 treats autonomy itself as the source of danger rather than as a lever on exposure. Distractor 2 wrongly treats unlocking a higher autonomy level as an obligation to use it. Distractor 3 smuggles in a capability change the scenario explicitly rules out. (Defining and Measuring AGI -> Defining General Intelligence)
candidate.takeaway: Autonomy is a deployment-time choice layered on capability, not a symptom or a requirement of it.

self_check.cover_test: Yes - a reader who has separated capability from autonomy can state that risk exposure differs here while capability does not, without seeing the options.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might pick whichever option calls the more autonomous setting inherently more dangerous, since that matches intuition, but the explanation specifically corrects the inherent-versus-exposure conflation.
